News Podcast Luxury condo was built where it’s not supposed to be 1 Now the City of Sarasota has to figure out what to do with Villa Ballada. By Noah Bookstein Original Air Date: August 20, 2026 Host: Villa Ballada is the latest luxury condo addition to Sarasota’s fast-gentrifying Rosemary District. Construction has been completed, and the city issued a certificate of occupancy. Its 22 apartments are up for sale, starting at $1 million a pop—and there’s retail space, too, downstairs. But there’s a small problem: It’s been built where it is not supposed to be. WLSR’s Noah Bookstein reports. Noah Bookstein: In downtown Sarasota’s Rosemary District, down the block from WSLR studios, a five-story condo building called Villa Ballada has been sitting about a foot into public land on Kumquat Court—for over a year—without anyone catching it. Last month, the city commission wanted to know how that happened and who pays for it. Villa Ballada’s foundation was poured slightly skewed to the west of where it was supposed to be, which pushed the building into the public, city-owned land along Kumquat Court. At its widest point, the encroachment is just over a foot. At its narrowest, under eight inches. All together, it adds up to about a hundred square feet of public land the building is now sitting on. At a city commission meeting last month, City Building Official Larry Murphy gave commissioners an explanation of how it happened. Larry Murphy: Obviously, the contractor of record and the developer at the time didn’t have their control lines, and they missed the layout of the building. It’s not like it hasn’t happened in history. Any time you have humans involved, you can have human error. NB: Commissioners were stunned at how a mistake of this size happened in the first place and went undetected for a year of construction. Vice Mayor Kathy Kelley Ohlrich said she was “beside herself.” Kathy Kelley Ohlrich: I have to say that I’m absolutely beside myself about this. I’m so perplexed. I can’t even believe how on Earth something like this could happen. NB: Murphy said a check called a spot survey, which would have caught the misalignment early, wasn’t actually mandatory at the time. City officials described it as a “passive stop” in the permitting process—meaning inspections could continue even without it. The encroachment itself is small enough that inspectors reviewing the site as the building went up did not flag it. The developer also used several different general contractors over the course of construction. City officials said that kind of turnover makes it easier for a detail like this to fall through the cracks between teams. According to Murphy, the city has already changed its process because of the incident. LM: What used to be a passive on the spot survey has now become a hard stop. No one can go past that any longer. NB: Even after the cause was explained, commissioners recognized the agreement in front of them would have let the developer keep using that hundred square feet of public land—permanently—without paying the city anything for it. The vice mayor’s reaction: KKO: Who thought that was a good idea? NB: During the meeting, the commission began asking what the public should get in return for the encroachment. Debbie Trice: What I want to focus on for right now is: How do we compensate the public for the loss? NB: Commissioners rejected the agreement and sent it back, directing the city manager and city attorney to negotiate something more equitable. Negotiations between the city, the Rosemary District Association and the developer have been underway for the past several weeks—largely out of public view. Emails obtained by WSLR show the city looping in Melissa Laughlin, president of the Rosemary District Association, just over a week after the commission’s vote. Laughlin had sent city staff a list of neighborhood priorities and the city is still pulling together cost estimates for the developer. The Rosemary District Association, after consulting local organizations including WSLR and Fogartyville, lists improved lighting along the full block and an extension of lighting Lemon Lane. They are also requesting additional parking, which generated the most emphatic response from nearby businesses, and they are seeking sidewalk repairs, especially the brick section outside Resurrection House. According to emails, the developer of Villa Ballada originally had roughly five street parking spaces right outside the building—but the city had instructed them to remove those spaces and put in landscaping instead. The Rosemary District Association declined to comment further for this story, saying negotiations with the city and developer are still ongoing. The hearing remains open, with no date yet set for it to return to the commission. Villa Ballada is built by Czech developer Karel Dudych of DBD Group. WSLR reached out to the developer for comment, but no response was given by deadline. When Commissioner Jen Ahearn-Koch pressed a representative for Dudych, Jacob Pendleton, to say directly who was responsible, he offered a stark admission. Jen Ahearn-Koch: I’m trying to figure out who is ultimately at fault here. Who is responsible for this error? Jacob Pendleton: It would be the developer. I mean, it’s us. It’s on our shoulders. NB: For WSLR News, Noah Bookstein. WSLR News aims to keep the local community informed with our 1/2 hour local news show, quarterly newspaper and social media feeds. The local news broadcast airs on Tuesdays and Thursday at 6pm. He also noted that, following this difficult phase, the country would enter a “growth phase” and that he was considering easing certain fiscal consolidation measures as soon as Romania can afford to do so. Also on Friday, in a press statement, he announced the start of drafting the government program in collaboration with the PNL, USR, and UDMR, noting that he would present the priorities early next week. He emphasized that Romania needs “a serious, credible government as soon as possible, a government that continues the reform measures, projects, and programs initiated over the past year.” While the official nomination of Liberal Siegfried Mureşan for the role of Prime Minister will take place on Monday, the three supporting parties have already begun the process of forming the cabinet and outlining the government program, tasks that must be completed within ten days. Siegfried Mureşan needs the support of 233 members of parliament, whereas the three parties backing him hold a combined total of 170 seats. Meanwhile, the PSD has called on the Prime Minister designate to publicly present his plan for Romania, including economic measures to protect the population and support Romanian companies, before any discussions regarding parliamentary majorities take place. The nationalist opposition party AUR also does not support him. For his part, Nicuşor Dan urged parliamentary parties to focus on forming a new government and called for a solution to be found. Summit – Carpathian countries must cooperate more effectively to build roads and border crossings, strengthen energy connections, promote tourism and economic and cultural exchanges, protect nature, and attract investment, stated President Nicuşor Dan, who attended the first Summit of the Carpathian Integration Initiative on Friday. “Romania is home to half of the Carpathian mountain range, and our involvement is therefore significant,” Nicuşor Dan wrote on social media. Additionally, Nicuşor Dan held a bilateral meeting on Friday with his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to discuss the need to fast-track the joint drone production project under the SAFE Program. According to the Romanian head of state, discussions also covered the transit of grain from Ukraine through Romania. “We also discussed grain transit, both by rail and via the Danube, to see how we can make it more efficient. It is a transit flow that generates substantial revenue for Romanian companies,” Nicuşor Dan noted. The head of state attended the meeting in the Ukrainian region of Ivano-Frankivsk at the invitation of the President of Ukraine, alongside representatives from the countries spanned by the Carpathian Mountains, Austria, the Czech Republic, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Ukraine, as well as other key players in regional cooperation. Meeting – Europe has entered a phase where it can no longer afford to delay decisions, and Romania’s ambitions must rise significantly, this was the key takeaway from the two-day EU finance ministers’ meeting (ECOFIN) in Dublin, according to a social media post by the interim Finance Minister Alexandru Nazare. He noted that Romania’s economic growth has slowed in recent years; therefore, financing costs must be reduced and domestic investment made more attractive. In his view, Romania needs more than just a way to navigate the next budget cycle or the next crisis; it requires a clear direction for the coming decade. While in Dublin, Alexandru Nazare met with his EU counterparts and held discussions with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann, EIB President Nadia Calviño, and European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis. Their talks focused on the need for Europe to increase investment, better mobilize private capital, and regain its productivity edge. Elections – The Romanian Foreign Ministry condemns the holding of elections for the State Duma of the Russian Federation, between September 18 and 20, in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as the opening of polling stations in the Transdniestr region of the Republic of Moldova without the consent of the authorities in Chișinău. According to a Foreign Ministry statement, holding elections in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine constitutes a serious violation of international law. Romania reaffirms its firm support for the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova within their internationally recognized borders, and rejects any unilateral action by which the Russian Federation seeks to undermine the international legal order, the statement adds. Bucharest Days – Bucharest Days are being celebrated this Saturday and Sunday. The event features concerts, performances, video mapping projections, guided tours, and debates, marking 567 years since the city’s first documentary attestation, according to the Capital’s City Hall.
